title: The hands
hook: the cosmic mudra: left hand on right, thumbs lightly touching, an oval at the navel

segments.voice: Yesterday, zazen: a stable base, ears over shoulders, nose over navel. Your line: straight and relaxed.

Hands are hardly ever off duty. Since waking they've probably held a phone, a cup, a door handle, a spoon; typed, scrolled, pointed, waved. Even resting, they fidget. Sit down to meditate and they get restless: on the knees, then the thighs, then folded, then back on the knees. Zen gives them a job, a very small one, done resting in the lap.
screen: `HANDS ARE NEVER OFF DUTY.` → `EVEN RESTING, THEY FIDGET.` → `ZEN GIVES THEM A JOB.`

segments.voice: In zazen the hands rest in the lap in what's often called the cosmic mudra. A mudra is a gesture held with the hands, sometimes called a seal. The back of one hand rests in the palm of the other, fingers overlapping, the left on the right in the usual Soto Zen instruction. Dogen's guide to sitting gives it that way. The tips of the two thumbs come up and just meet over the fingers, lightly. Some teachers say: as if holding a sheet of paper between them. Hands and thumbs make an oval that rests against the belly, near the navel. Here's the clever part. The thumbs are a small gauge. If they press together into a peak, there's probably tension somewhere: effort, trying too hard. If they sag apart into a valley, the mind may be getting dull or drowsy. So some teachers say: don't stare at the mind, check the thumbs. They show the strain before it's noticed anywhere else. With the hands joined and resting, the arms can drop from the shoulders, and the fidgeting has nowhere to go. The hands aren't asleep. They hold a shape that takes almost no effort and just a little attention. Some statues of the Buddha seated in meditation show a resting gesture like this one, a way of saying with the body: nothing to grab right now, nothing to push away.
screen: `ONE HAND RESTING IN THE OTHER.` · `THUMBS JUST TOUCHING.` · `THE THUMBS ARE A GAUGE.` · `NOTHING TO GRAB.` · then, large: `AN OVAL AT THE NAVEL.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and relaxed, lay one hand in the other, left resting on right, and bring the thumb tips up until they just touch, the oval resting near your belly. Keep a little attention in the thumbs: if they press, soften; if they drift apart, gently bring them back. That's the whole job.
The hands. In zazen, the cosmic mudra: one hand resting in the other, thumbs lightly touching, an oval near the navel. Today's word.
Your line: thumbs just touching. A small shape, and a quiet gauge. Day twelve hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: In Zen sitting, practitioners usually hold the hands in the cosmic mudra for the whole period, and teachers check beginners' hands along with their posture.

chat.meaning: In the cosmic mudra the thumbs just touch; some teachers say pressing shows tension and sagging shows dullness, so the thumbs show strain early.

notes: No quotations. Hand order: Soto/Dogen gives left hand on right palm (right hand on left foot first in lotus); some Rinzai teachers reverse it. Lesson says 'in the usual Soto Zen instruction'; confirm.
The 'sheet of paper' image and the peak/valley gauge are common teaching images, attributed to teachers generally; confirm.
'Cosmic mudra' is the common English name for hokkai join (法界定印); consider adding the Japanese name.
Statement that seated Buddha statues often show a resting meditation gesture: kept general.
